/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.headline: Macron says ‘welcome back’ to Burnham suggestion UK could rejoin EU
/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.excerpt: The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has reacted warmly to Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could rejoin the EU. “Welcome back,” the French leader said in English with a smile at a news conference in Madrid on Wednesday. Macron continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said his country would open its arms to any bid from the UK to rejoin the EU. The two leaders were responding to the British prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference in which Burnham said Britain would not have a clear path “until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market” and that Brexit had “done more harm than good”. In a series of interviews on Wednesday, Burnham said the government could maintain the status quo, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” for full EU membership. Macron said the British had “always been useful in helping us simplify things” when the UK was part of the EU and were “demanding partners”. Burnham “is right to have this boldness”, he added. Earlier, Macron, who has frequently accused the proponents of Brexit of misleading the public, said Brexit had been “the biggest lie of the last 30 years”, pointing to shortfalls in promised economic growth and trade opportunities.
/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.trail: French president, speaking alongside Spanish counterpart Pedro Sánchez, says EU bid would be good news for UK and Europeans

/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.headline: Andy Burnham wants to review the UK’s relationship with the EU. What are the options?
/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.excerpt: Andy Burnham has said Brexit has “done more harm than good” and pledged to launch a major review of the UK’s relationship with the EU, opening the door to a potential referendum over rejoining the union. He said he would “lay out options” around the time of the next EU-UK summit, due to be held at the end of November or soon after. While he didn’t specify options, he did not explicitly rule out rejoining. Keir Starmer’s red lines of not rejoining the single market or customs union could now also be up for discussion within Labour’s ranks in the coming weeks. “I would be stunned if Starmer’s red lines are in the next manifesto,” said Joël Reland, senior research fellow at UK in a Changing Europe, a key Brexit thinkthank. What exactly did Burnham say on the EU? “Brexit hasn’t given us control,” he said, arguing the UK had not just lost control of immigration – contrary to what Brexiters had promised – but also over the economy. “I will take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long term relationship with our European partners,” he said. “There are different options and I will see if we can find consensus around one, which will give us clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in.” Why is this significant?
/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.trail: The PM said Brexit has ‘done more harm than good’ and wants an assessment before the next UK-EU summit

/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.headline: ‘We’ve done everything by the book’: EU citizens left in limbo after UK government strips post-Brexit residency status
/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.excerpt: The Home Office faces legal action over a policy to strip residency rights from EU citizens who were in the UK before Brexit on the grounds that it gave them the status “in error”. It comes as a Home Office minister revealed that the government has contacted 1,473 citizens with post-Brexit residency rights to tell them the original decision to grant them residency was made in error. The campaign group the3million, which is aware of at least 50 cases, has put the Home Office on notice that it is seeking a judicial review of the policy, which it enacted in late 2025 but has only recently come to light. “In many cases, the Home Office is actually wrong to say there was a mistake. So people whose status was properly granted are now fighting not to lose it – this is a clear breach of the withdrawal agreement,” it said in an appeal to supporters to fund their case. Some of those who received notice were told they were not entitled to pre-settled or settled status because they did not submit passports with their original application. This includes a group of Brazilians and others with dual Italian nationality by birth whom the Home Office claimed were not Italian at the time of their pre-Brexit residency applications. Among them is a 33-year-old Italian engineer who has been in London since 2018, when he arrived for a PhD, and now has “settled status” – permanent residency granted after five years.
/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.trail: Home Office faces legal action after 1,473 people living in UK before Brexit told settled status was granted in error

/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.headline: UK ‘losing up to £6.5bn a year in EU trade’ without post-Brexit product deal
/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.excerpt: The UK is losing out on annual exports to the EU that could be worth as much as £6.5bn without a deal with Brussels that allows manufacturers to jettison duplicate product testing. In the latest attempt to calculate the loss of trade with the EU after Brexit, the IPPR thinktank said many companies have given up selling goods to the EU or set up subsidiaries inside the trade bloc after successive governments failed to secure a mutual recognition agreement that would avoid the extra administration costs. The thinktank estimated that the absence of such a deal may have cost UK exporters between £3.7bn and £6.5bn each year in lost revenue since the UK’s post-Brexit trading arrangements came into force in 2021. It urged the government to reopen talks with the EU, saying that the loss of trade amounted to about 0.18% of annual national income, or about three times what the UK government expects to gain from its trade deal with Japan, Canada, Australia and Singapore, known as the CPTPP deal. At this week’s Liberal Democrat conference, the party’s leader, Ed Davey, said that should the party take control at Westminster, he would begin talks to rejoin the EU single market and customs union. He said the move would bring the UK into alignment with its largest trading partner, boost exports and kickstart growth. Earlier this year, the Starmer administration pitched the creation of a single market for goods between the UK and EU to Brussels, but the proposal was rejected by EU officials.
/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.trail: IPPR finds failure to align testing standards costing 0.18% of national income and has seen companies abandon exporting to EU

/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.headline: Tony Blair says Britain should work towards rejoining EU in next 10 years
/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.excerpt: Britain should work towards rejoining the EU in the next decade, Tony Blair has said, adding to growing pressure on Andy Burnham to abandon Labour’s reluctance to revisit the 2016 referendum. The former prime minister has urged Burnham to use his 10-year plan in November to put the country’s membership of the union back on the table, a decade after it voted to leave. In a paper entitled A Path to Rejoining a Reformed Europe, the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) calls for the UK to accept free movement of people and make a financial contribution as the price of entry. The intervention comes after Burnham declined to rule out promising to rejoin the EU in the next Labour manifesto, though it also threatens to reopen the deep rifts caused by the vote 10 years ago. In a foreword to the paper, Blair argues: “Britain should signal an intention if the terms are right to enter into a structured formal relationship with Europe and initiate a process of negotiation where everything is on the table but nothing agreed until everything is agreed.” TBI researchers say in the paper itself: “Over the next decade, Britain should work towards the ambition of rejoining a significantly reformed EU.” Blair is the latest in a series of Labour figures to back rejoining the EU.
/politics/2026/sep/30/no-10-gathering-ev.trail: Andy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chances

/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.headline: Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant
/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.excerpt: Three decades ago, it took the deaths of three children from a Roman Catholic family – the Quinn brothers, Jason, nine, Mark, 10, and 11-year-old Richard – in a petrol bomb attack to bring an end to the Drumcree dispute. “No road is worth a life, let alone the lives of three little boys,” the Orange Order’s County Armagh chaplain said at the time. It is perhaps extraordinary to think that this could ever have needed saying – but that was then. Northern Ireland is very different place today. Passions are running high, but the attempt by 35 members of the Protestant Orange Order to walk down Garvaghy Road, a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist part of Drumcree in Portadown, County Armagh, did not lead to violence on Sunday or Monday. Faced with thousands of members of the nationalist community standing in their way and a police line ordering them back, Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson concluded: “There’s no point getting wet unnecessarily,” as he instructed members of the order back inside the church hall to shelter from the rain. Every half-hour on Monday, the Orange Order members walked up to police lines only to be turned back by Supt Brendan Green, but the process was peaceful and respectful. The blessed absence of the old ways does not make what is happening at Drumcree any less significant, however. History doesn’t repeat itself, and although hope and history sometimes rhyme, more often we hear echoes of history returning to us.
/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.trail: Row comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland

/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.headline: Tensions rise as Orange Order members vow to continue with march blocked by police
/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.excerpt: Tensions between unionist and nationalist leaders in Northern Ireland have escalated as a number of Orange Order members remain at Drumcree church, vowing not to leave until they can proceed with their march down a nationalist road in Portadown. Members of the loyalist Orange Lodge made a third attempt to proceed down Garvaghy Road at 4am on Monday morning, but a line of police Land Rovers blocked their path. While protesters at the head of Garvaghy Road were dispersed late last night, there are fears that the tensions between Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) have reached a level that could lead to the collapse of power sharing at Stormont. Speaking to the Irish broadcaster RTÉ on Monday morning, Claire Hanna, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party, said collapsing Stormont “solves nothing” as it would halt critical decision-making. “Too often, we have reached for these collapse mechanisms only to have to come back six months later,” she said. The leader of the Ulster Unionist party, Jon Burrows, also said he did not “want to see the executive fall”. He told the BBC: “There are people waiting for health appointments, there are people that wait too long in A&E, people that wait too long for an ambulance, there are lots of initiatives that [health] minister [Robbie] Butler and his predecessors need delivered.
/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.trail: Talks expected on Monday after Sinn Féin leaders join those on streets opposing decision to allow unionist parade for first time since 1998

/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.headline: Loyalist parade in Northern Ireland given go-ahead as almost 30-year ban overturned
/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.excerpt: A controversial loyalist parade along a nationalist street in the Northern Ireland town of Portadown is set to go ahead for the first time in nearly 30 years, after an overnight court ruling cleared it to proceed. The Orange Order parade down the Garvaghy Roadis scheduled for 8am on Sunday morning, and follows a last-minute legal back-and-forth. Northern Ireland was blighted for three decades by conflict between largely Catholic, pro-Irish republicans and Protestant, pro-UK unionists, and the Garvaghy Road became a major flashpoint during the late 1990s. After a five-hour hearing at a special sitting of the high court on Saturday, Justice Patricia Smyth issued an order temporarily suspending the parade. Smyth had urged all sides to “step back from the abyss” and take responsible decisions for “the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland”. But at 11.30pm on Saturday, at a sitting of the court of appeals, Lady Chief Justice Siobhan Keegan said the high court judge who granted the injunction against the march had “unfortunately erred in law”. A new application at the high court to stop the Protestant parade from passing through the Catholic area was also dismissed in the early hours of Sunday morning. The time-limited sitting beginning at 12.20am on Sunday was heard before Justice Michael Humphreys who acknowledged the “unusual if not unprecedented circumstances of the last-minute proceedings.
/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.trail: Orange Order march along Garvaghy Road scheduled to take place for first time in 28 years after injunction dismissed on appeal

/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.headline: Jeffrey Donaldson could face more than 10 years in jail for child sexual abuse, court told
/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.excerpt: Jeffrey Donaldson, the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party in Northern Ireland, could be sent to prison for more than 10 years over the sexual assault of two women when they were children, a court heard on Friday. The disgraced politician, who headed the DUP between 2021 and 2024, was found guilty of 18 counts of sexual abuse including one count of rape against the women in June. Recounting the case, Rosemary Walsh KC reminded Judge Ramsey how the distress felt by Complainant B while giving evidence was “palpable” in the court room. Referring to a victim statement already with the judge, she told how Complainant B had described the trial as “a terrible experience” and how the abuse she suffered as a child “affected her every day” of her life. Sometimes she struggled so much she “wishes she could die”, Walsh said, adding that as a result of the abuse she “does not know what love and trust really is”. The other victim, Complainant A, wrote in her victim impact statement that she felt her childhood had been “stolen from her” and this had led to feelings of shame and anger. Her sleep and sense of wellbeing were affected to this day and sometimes she felt burnt out from the emotional stress. Walsh spoke of various tariffs for the offences, several of which carried a maximum sentence of two years, but others which carried a maximum sentence of between 10 and 14 years under historical tariffs for crimes, she told the court.
/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.trail: Age difference between former Democratic Unionist party leader and his victims an aggravating factor, say prosecutors

/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.headline: Westminster’s time is coming to an end, say first ministers of UK’s Celtic nations
/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.excerpt: Westminster’s time is coming to an end, the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have said at a summit aimed at putting the UK’s Celtic nations on the path to independence referendums. The Plaid Cymru leader, Rhun ap Iorwerth; the Scottish National party leader, John Swinney; Sinn Féin’s vice-president, Michelle O’Neill, and the president and leader of the opposition in Ireland, Mary Lou McDonald, met in Cardiff on Monday to sign a memorandum of understanding recognising that “the political landscape across these islands is changing”. “Momentum is behind our movements; we believe that constitutional change is coming,” the memorandum read. “No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future. “We call for the British government to prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction.” Since becoming prime minister in July, Andy Burnham has put regional devolution of power and resources in England at the heart of his agenda, but policy towards the devolved administrations has so far been muddled. The summit was the first face-to-face meeting for the sister parties since Plaid Cymru won May’s Senedd elections, which put separatist parties in government in all three countries for the first time. The leaders met in their capacity as party, rather than government, officials, discussing economic, energy and international cooperation as well as self-determination.
/uk-news/2026/sep/30/garvaghy-road-march.trail: Leaders in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland discuss independence and call for constitutional change at summit

/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.headline: NAZA film-makers address threats at documentary’s New York City premiere
/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.excerpt: The film-makers behind NAZA, the award-winning documentary on Israel’s systemic mass killing of Palestinians in Gaza, defended their findings at the film’s North American premiere in New York on Saturday, amid protests in Israel and escalating threats from Israeli officials to strip them of their citizenship. The critically acclaimed film, directed by Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, features the testimony of 24 anonymized Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, who describe the AI-powered systems used to select their targets. The project takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike, which are often conducted at night in private homes, killing many family members, including children, at once. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience at the New York film festival in a Q&A that followed the film’s premiere. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.” “These crimes that you saw are ongoing,” Abraham said.
/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.trail: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor defend findings on Israel’s killing of Palestinians amid threats from Israeli officials

/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.headline: Netanyahu’s speech at UN spurs protests in New York City: ‘Let Gaza live’
/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.excerpt: More than 100 people were arrested outside the United Nations’ headquarters in New York City on Thursday as Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the general assembly, a speech that also prompted dozens of UN delegates to walk out in protest. The protest outside the UN, one of several this week against the embattled Israeli prime minister, drew hundreds of Jewish, Palestinian, Iranian and Lebanese New Yorkers, among others, as well as several elected officials and candidates in the November election, and a number of celebrities. Many wore shirts reading “Fund people not bombs” and chanted slogans like “Let Gaza live” and “the whole world is watching.” Official vehicles heading to the UN were diverted as protesters sat down in the middle of the street for more than an hour, unfurling banners that called to “end the genocide” and flying a kite reading “Free Palestine” – a reference to Israel’s threat earlier this year that it would target Palestinian children flying kites, organizers said. A few hours later, an estimated few thousand people marched from nearby Bryant Park to the UN in protest of Netanyahu’s visit to the city. Swathed in keffiyehs and carrying Palestinian flags, accompanied by a brass band and drummers, protesters held banners calling on UN member states to sanction Israel, others with illustrations of Netanyahu’s face.
/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.trail: Actor Susan Sarandon, whistleblower Chelsea Manning and comedian Caleb Hearon are detained by NYPD

/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.headline: Global release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZA
/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.excerpt: NAZA, the award-winning documentary from Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is set to be released in cinemas in more than 50 countries before a digital global release on theguardian.com. The film, which the Guardian produced, premiered at the Venice film festival earlier this month, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize. After screenings in Bologna and at the San Sebastián film festival, the film will receive its North American premiere on Saturday at the New York film festival before opening four days later at the IFC Center in New York City. On 9 October it will expand to Los Angeles and other key US cities before a national rollout. A theatrical release in partnership with MK2 Films is also planned in 55 other territories, including the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Canada, Hong Kong, Brazil, Turkey, Thailand, France, Spain, Germany, Turkey, Central America and the Middle East. After its run in cinemas, the film will stream in late November on the Guardian’s website, for free, as part of the news organisation’s commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism. “NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years,” said Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and one of NAZA’s producers.
/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.trail: Theatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian website

/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.headline: Charlotte Church accuses Ed Sheeran of ‘choosing capitalism over doing the right thing’
/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.excerpt: Charlotte Church has accused Ed Sheeran of choosing “consumerism and capitalism over doing the right thing” over the removal of his friend and support act Macklemore from his US tour. Sheeran’s tour was thrown into crisis after Macklemore made “free Palestine” declarations on stage. After a significant backlash, including pressure from the owners of stadiums hosting scheduled shows, the rapper was removed from the tour. Shortly afterwards, Sheeran’s other support acts quit in solidarity. Sheeran addressed the controversy during his concert in Philadelphia on Saturday, saying what was happening in Gaza was “catastrophic and unjustifiable”. He apologised to fans, saying: “I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I’m so, so sorry.” He added that he wanted his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics. Church, who has previously been vocal about her support for Palestinians, said: “Ed Sheeran, we’re watching you,” during a gig in Cardiff on Sunday, and urged the audience to chant “free Palestine”. She said: “Whilst he [Sheeran] has made millions and has an enormous following – he has an enormous platform to do real good in the world – he chose consumerism and capitalism over doing the right thing. “So we say the same thing to Ed Sheeran because fuck the fact that musicians shouldn’t be involved in politics. Fuck that shit.
/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.trail: Church, a prominent supporter of Palestinian causes, criticises Sheeran over removal of Macklemore from US tour

/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.headline: Ed Sheeran says situation in Gaza ‘unjustifiable’ in first show since tour plunged into turmoil
/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.excerpt: Ed Sheeran has opened a solo concert in Philadelphia with comments about Gaza, saying what is happening is “catastrophic and unjustifiable”, in his first show since his tour was plunged into turmoil. “My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’ lives, of children’s lives,” Sheeran said on Saturday, adding that he wanted his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics. The singer said he had been unsure “whether this tour would be carrying on” and “whether I even wanted to be an artist at all” after criticism that had been levelled at him. Outside the stadium a small gathering of chanting protesters greeted concertgoers, waving Palestinian flags and chanting “free, free Palestine”. Sheeran’s US Loop tour has been embroiled in crisis since the rapper Macklemore was removed as opening act on Monday, after the owners of stadiums hosting coming shows objected to his shouting “free Palestine” on stage in New Jersey earlier this month. Sheeran, 35, has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore, instead blaming the tour promoter. Four supporting acts subsequently withdrew from the tour, issuing public statements citing their support for Palestinians. Sheeran’s backing band, Beoga, also announced they were stepping down, sharing a statement on Instagram that said they “fully supported” Macklemore’s message. The start time for the Philadelphia show was pushed back from 5.30pm local time to 8pm, according to Ticketmaster.
/world/2026/oct/01/new-google-maps-image.trail: Pop star has faced boycott calls since rapper Macklemore was removed from tour after shouting ‘free Palestine’ at concert

/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.headline: After four killings and a revealing autopsy, Memphis is fed up with the national guard takeover
/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.excerpt: National guard troops began walking the streets of Memphis a year ago this week, as part of a federal surge of law enforcement agents sent into the city at the behest of the Trump administration to reduce violent crime. Fewer soldiers are on the street today, as the city’s grudging initial acceptance of the president’s deployment has given way to doubts about their effectiveness, focus and respect for civil rights – particularly after four men were killed in gunfire by federal agents working with the taskforce, with a recent autopsy showing that one was shot in the back. Donald Trump signed an executive order last September directing a surge of federal law enforcement agents from the ATF, FBI, Department of Homeland Security and other agencies into Memphis. A month later, Tennessee’s Republican governor, Bill Lee, paired that with additional state patrol officers and the activation of 1,500 Tennessee national guard members to patrol the streets of downtown Memphis. The Memphis Safe Task Force claims credit for deep reductions in the violent crime rate. And while the city is on track for the lowest rate of homicides in decades, independent analysis argues the deployment of the national guard has had no statistically measurable impact on violent crime and that violence would have fallen in Memphis much like it has across the country in cities without similar interventions. Memphis’s headline-driving homicide rate has fallen about 35% since the start of the taskforce.
/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.trail: Although state officials laud a reduction in violent crime, a report claims it would have happened without the taskforce

/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.headline: Louisiana man allegedly killed his wife and drove her body across states before arrest
/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.excerpt: A man in Louisiana killed his wife and then took her body on a driving tour through several states before he was arrested in Tennessee, authorities allege. The suspect’s macabre purported odyssey began in Baton Rouge when, according to Louisiana investigators, Tyronne Brazille, 50, shot dead his wife, Lanessa Bradford, also 50, during an argument at the city’s Independence Community Park. Instead of contacting law enforcement officials, Brazille decided to strap her body into the passenger seat of his car and embark on a five-hour, almost 400-mile (644km) drive north to Tennessee. They passed through Mississippi before the road trip ended in downtown Memphis, where police pulled the vehicle over for a traffic violation – and discovered Bradford deceased with a gunshot wound. Brazille was arrested as a fugitive and will appear at an extradition hearing in Memphis on Monday. He faces a count of second-degree murder in Louisiana, his arrest warrant states. According to Bradford’s longtime friend, Shelicka Decker, who spoke to the Memphis CBS News affiliate WREG, the elementary school employee was married to Brazille for a number of years – but the couple was experiencing difficulties and she recently told him she was going to leave. “She had the money saved up,” Decker said. “She had come up with a plan, and she was going to just vanish. “That was the only way she would be able to get away from him.
/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.trail: Authorities say man, 50, shot wife in Louisiana and put her body in car before driving and being stopped in Tennessee

/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.headline: NAACP demands end of Trump’s anticrime taskforce in Memphis after deaths of Black men
/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.excerpt: The deaths in recent days of two Black men in Tennessee, one in the custody of police and the other at the hands of national guard troops, has prompted the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People to demand the suspension of the so-called Memphis Safe Task Force, Donald Trump’s anti-crime alliance of federal, state and local law enforcement. In a letter to the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, on Friday, the NAACP also demanded “a thorough, transparent federal investigation” into the actions of the taskforce, which it said has surged federal and military officers into Memphis with insufficient training for civilian policing. The action follows the death by shooting of Tyrin Johnson, a 20-year-old new father, by two Tennessee national guard troops in an early morning incident on Sunday; and the discovery of the body of Darius Chappell, a 34-year-old father of three young sons, in a cell at the Montgomery county jail two days earlier. Chappell was taken into custody on 29 June after what police said was a “use of force” incident in Clarksville. Video of his violent arrest circulating on social media showed a police dog appearing to bite him while he was being held on the ground by several officers. Authorities have revealed few details about either incident. In Johnson’s case, the Tennessee bureau of investigation (TBI) asserted he had been in possession of a handgun and had fired shots.
/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.trail: Advocacy group calls on acting attorney general to lead ‘thorough, transparent federal investigation’

/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.headline: Tennessee national guard troops shoot man dead in Memphis
/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.excerpt: National guard soldiers on patrol in Memphis shot and killed a man that authorities in the Tennessee city said turned and pulled a gun on the troops during a chase. The shooting took place at about 4am on Sunday as the soldiers responded to a report of gunfire. The Tennessee national guard was deployed controversially by the state’s governor, Bill Lee, in October to support the federal push by Donald Trump, his fellow Republican, to tackle perceived crime surges in Democratic-run cities. According to the Tennessee bureau of investigation (TBI), the man shot was Tyrin Johnson, 20. The bureau said nobody else was hurt during the shooting – and that it was looking into the circumstances. “For reasons under investigation, the situation escalated, resulting in two national guard soldiers firing upon Johnson, striking and killing him,” the TBI said in a statement. It did not identify the soldiers involved and directed inquiries “to the respective department to answer as it sees fit”. Lt Col Darrin Haas, spokesperson for the Tennessee national guard, also declined to identify the personnel involved. He told the Associated Press in a statement that Johnson died at the scene after two national guard medical specialists attempted first aid. Memphis’s mayor, Paul Young, a Democrat, said the shooting was an “unfortunate incident”.
/us-news/2026/sep/30/tennessee-execution.trail: Authorities claim Tyrin Johnson, 20, pulled gun on officers controversially deployed at instigation of Trump

/music/2026/oct/01/oasis-legal-action-sa.headline: The Guide #260: From Oasis to K-pop, music is going mad for the big-screen documentary
/music/2026/oct/01/oasis-legal-action-sa.excerpt: There’s a moment towards the end of Don’t Look Back in Anger, the newly released documentary capturing Oasis’s 2025 reunion tour, that helps explain why those planet-conquering gigs happened in the first place. Liam and Noel Gallagher are sitting down together for the rarest of paired interviews – the first since the 2009 scrap that broke up the band and created such a huge appetite for their return. Had Oasis’s story ended with that backstage fight in Paris, both Gallaghers note, their legacy would have been one of astonishing success curtailed by “chaos”. Instead, those reunion gigs, as well as proving wildly lucrative, have allowed them to add a triumphant coda to that messy ending. “It feels like a weight has been lifted,” a surprisingly contemplative Liam says. That maybe makes Don’t Look Back in Anger sound more navel-gazing than this entertaining and often very funny film is – as you might expect of any doc that features a sweary rumination from Noel on Liam’s ability to balance a tambourine on his head (“If I did that I’d look an utter cunt, but somehow he does it and it’s the greatest thing I’ve ever seen”). Still, for all the droll quippery and bucket-hatted euphoria, there is something poignant and self-reflective at the film’s heart: hatchets are buried, departed friends are toasted and legacies are contemplated. What you leave behind was clearly on the minds of the brothers Gallagher throughout the tour and film.

/music/2026/oct/01/oasis-legal-action-sa.headline: ‘Would they fight or hug?’ The Oasis comeback film’s makers on shooting fans, vicars, police – and the Gallaghers
/music/2026/oct/01/oasis-legal-action-sa.excerpt: On 4 July last year, Oasis were all set to start the first gig of their hugely anticipated comeback, 16 years since the band imploded after Liam Gallagher swung a guitar in the direction of brother Noel’s head backstage in Paris. However, just 20 minutes before showtime, there was no sign of the singer. Some 74,500 fans in Cardiff’s Principality Stadium were going crazy, while Noel was left impatiently pacing around the venue’s loading bay, presumably wondering if everything was about to fall apart again. “Then the monitor I was watching all this on suddenly cut out,” says Will Lovelace, the director who was filming the comeback. “When it came back to life, suddenly Liam and Noel were there chatting. Then they walked out to this eruption.” Later, Noel is filmed expressing incredulity that his long-estranged younger sibling could “skip the final rehearsal, then just rock up, grab my hand, and I’m like, ‘What the fuck?’ And off he goes, sounding like he’s 30 years younger. And I’m like, ‘You absolute mad cunt.’” The Cardiff entrance is one of the more dramatic scenes in Lovelace and co-director Dylan Southern’s film Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger, which briefly dwells on how the fractious working-class Manchester tearaways became the biggest rock band in the world in the 1990s before concentrating on how, 30 years later, they did it all again. The Oasis Live 25 tour consisted of 41 concerts across 14 countries and five continents, playing to more than two million people.

/music/2026/oct/01/oasis-legal-action-sa.headline: Oasis reunion helps draw record 25m ‘music tourists’ to UK concerts
/music/2026/oct/01/oasis-legal-action-sa.excerpt: Big name artists including Oasis with their highly anticipated reunion tour, Coldplay and Beyoncé helped to attract a record number of fans to travel to watch live music last year, helped by a surge in overseas visitors at UK gigs. A report from the industry body UK Music estimated that 24.7 million “music tourists” attended concerts and festivals last year, up 4.8% on 2024, leading to an unprecedented £11.2bn of spending across the UK economy. The vast majority (85%) were UK music fans designated as “domestic tourists” because they travelled more than three times the average commute to go to an event. The number of overseas music tourists soared by 27% to 2.1 million, well up on the 1.6 million in 2024. Several major artists, including Coldplay, Lana Del Rey and Oasis, played only in the UK last year, helping drive overseas music tourist numbers. Music UK did not have data for overall gig attendees, but it is likely to be far higher when local fans are included. The report gave particular credit to the Gallagher brothers’ reunion tour – where Oasis played for the first time in 15 years – despite a scandal over ticket pricing for the most profitable run of gigs in British history. The band’s decision to play five gigs at Manchester’s Heaton Park led to music tourist spending in the north-west rising 16% year on year to £1.4bn.

/music/2026/oct/01/oasis-legal-action-sa.headline: ‘I was there!’ Writers remember legendary gigs by Beyoncé, Brian Wilson, Britney, Oasis, Daft Punk and more
/music/2026/oct/01/oasis-legal-action-sa.excerpt: ‘Every song was crisp and fully formed’ Talking Heads, the Rock Garden, London, 13 May 1977 Talking Heads broke off from a European tour supporting Ramones in 1977 to play two shows at the Rock Garden, a small basement club on the Covent Garden Piazza, now the site of an Apple Store. After an apprenticeship as a three-piece (David Byrne, Tina Weymouth, Chris Frantz), the band had recently added a fourth member, Jerry Harrison, and were close to completing work on their debut album. In London, every song was crisp and fully formed, with Psycho Killer as the set’s devastating climax. The audience included Brian Eno, who invited them to his flat the next day for a meeting that would lead to collaborations on More Songs About Buildings and Food, Fear of Music, Remain in Light and (as a Byrne/Eno project) My Life in the Bush of Ghosts: a series of albums that changed music. Richard Williams The sun shone out of their behinds The Smiths, The Refectory, University of Leeds, 29 February 1984 I remember what I wore: a 1950s charity shop raincoat, traditional black slacks and a “grandad” shirt from a vintage shop, dyed brown in a pan in our kitchen. This was topped off with an atrocious attempt at a quiff. So many of us scrambled to adopt the Smiths’s restyled retro chic because we wanted to be in their gang. In the nine months since their first single, Hand in Glove, they’d swept through John Peel/NME culture and into the Top 20.
